specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes enriching word-adjacency (co-occurrence) networks derived from speech transcripts with subword-aware word embeddings (Bojanowski et al., 2016) by adding semantic edges when cosine similarity exceeds a threshold (CNE). From these enriched graphs the authors compute aggregated node-level topological measures (mean, std, skew) for 10 network metrics, and use them as features in standard classifiers (SVM, RF, KNN, GaussianNB). They compare CNE against plain co-occurrence networks (CN), linguistic metrics (Coh-Metrix and Coh-Metrix-Dementia), and Bag-of-Words (tf), across three datasets (English Cookie Theft, Portuguese Cinderella (automatic and manually processed), and ABCD). Results (Tables 4–7) show CNE often matches or outperforms other single feature spaces and that majority-vote ensembles / multi-view majority-vote combinations sometimes yield further gains (notably Cinderella and ABCD). The manuscript argues CNE is more robust to disfluencies and short texts because semantic edges densify near-linear networks. However, critical methodological omissions limit certainty: no variance/confidence intervals for accuracies, unclear whether threshold/hyperparameter tuning was nested within cross-validation (risk of leakage/overfitting), limited ablations (no OOV statistics, no comparison to other embedding types or pretrained embeddings), and insufficient reporting of preprocessing lists and classifier tuning. Thus the empirical claim that CNE outperforms linguistic metrics is partially supported by point estimates in tables but uncertain in statistical and mechanistic terms.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Disfluent, short transcripts yield near-linear co-occurrence networks with weak discriminatory topology (cites Amancio 2015c).
A2: Adding semantic edges based on word embedding similarities densifies networks and captures semantic relations missing in co-occurrence-only graphs (method adapted from Perozzi et al. 2014).
A3: Subword-aware embeddings (Bojanowski et al.) reduce OOV problems in clinical/disfluent text and thus produce better similarity scores for semantic edges.
A4: Aggregated node-level topological measures (mean, std, skew) of enriched networks encode diagnostic signal relevant to MCI detection.
A5: Standard classifiers trained on these topological aggregates can distinguish MCI vs control with accuracy competitive to or better than Coh-Metrix / BoW baselines.
A6: Combining feature spaces (CNE, LM, BoW) via majority-vote ensembles / multi-view voting yields additional gains.
Conclusion: CNE is a practical, language-agnostic, parser-robust feature family for MCI detection from transcripts, especially when transcripts are noisy.

identified_claims.claim_text: Complex network representations of speech transcripts enriched with word embeddings (CNE) can be used to distinguish MCI from control participants with competitive classification accuracy across the tested datasets.
identified_claims.section_anchor: Abstract; Introduction; 5 Experiments and Results; 6 Conclusions
evidence: Abstract: statement asserting CNE can be used to distinguish MCI with competitive accuracy.
Section 5: Tables 4–7 show per-dataset accuracies where CNE is often the best single feature space (e.g., CNE entries in Tables 4–7).
Conclusion: restates that topological properties of CN outperform linguistic metrics in individual classifiers.
uncertainty_flags: No variance (SD/CI) or statistical significance tests provided for accuracies; single-point accuracy estimates do not quantify uncertainty.
Small dataset sizes (notably Cinderella) increase variance and possible overfitting; unclear if reported averages are stable.
Hyperparameter and threshold tuning procedures are underspecified (possible leakage if not nested in CV).

identified_claims.claim_label: CNE > linguistic metrics in noisy transcripts
identified_claims.claim_text: CNE features outperform traditional linguistic metrics (which rely on robust parsing) in the tested datasets, particularly when transcripts contain disfluencies and agrammatical structures.
identified_claims.section_anchor: Abstract; 4.2.2 Linguistic Features; 5 Experiments and Results; 6 Conclusions
evidence: Tables 4 and 5: CNE often outperforms LM (Coh-Metrix / Coh-Metrix-Dementia) in the automatic / uncorrected transcript versions.
Section 4.2.2: linguistic metrics dependent on parsing; authors removed parser-dependent LM metrics for Portuguese due to disfluencies.
Table 6: shows linguistic metrics perform well after manual transcript correction (supports dependence on transcript quality).
uncertainty_flags: No statistical testing reported to show differences are significant; observed differences may be within CV noise.
Manual correction experiment (Table 6) suggests LM can surpass CNE when transcripts are cleaned—so the advantage is conditional on transcript quality.
Processing choices (removing filled pauses, not lemmatizing) could differently affect LM and CNE, confounding the comparison.

identified_claims.claim_text: Combining feature types via ensemble and multi-view learning improves classification accuracy relative to individual classifiers, with notable gains reported on the Cinderella and ABCD datasets.
identified_claims.section_anchor: Abstract; 5 Experiments and Results; 6 Conclusions
evidence: Section 5 / Tables 5 and 7: ensemble and multiview rows show higher accuracies (e.g., Table 5: Ensemble CNE-LM = 0.75; Table 7: Ensemble CNE-LM-BoW = 0.7636, SVM-Linear CNE-LM-BoW = 0.8018).
Abstract: claims 10% improvement in Cinderella and 4.71% in Arizona dataset.
uncertainty_flags: Combining via majority vote is superficially described; lack of details whether ensemble combination used cross-validated predictions (to avoid overfitting) or applied on training folds directly.
Improvements measured as absolute percentages without uncertainty estimates; unclear if gains are robust.
Multi-view may benefit from simple aggregation here, but no exploration of weighted voting or stacking is reported.

identified_claims.claim_text: Using subword-aware embeddings (Bojanowski et al.) to enrich co-occurrence networks helps represent short texts more informatively, mitigating problems arising from short/transcriptional narratives and out-of-vocabulary words.
identified_claims.section_anchor: 3 Modeling and Characterizing Texts as Complex Networks; 4.2.1 Topological Characterization of Networks; 5 Experiments and Results
evidence: Section 3: rationale that short texts produce near-linear graphs and need enrichment.
Section 4.2.1: authors explicitly state they used Bojanowski et al. for OOV handling.
Section 5: CNE (enriched) often has higher accuracy than CN (co-occurrence only).
uncertainty_flags: No OOV statistics reported (rate of OOV tokens) or explicit ablation comparing Bojanowski to other embedding types (classic skip-gram, pretrained fastText, random features).
Only CN vs CNE comparison shown; the mechanism (OOV handling vs semantic densification) is not isolated.
Threshold selection for adding semantic edges is dataset-dependent and possibly tuned on evaluation folds; sensitivity unclear.

identified_claims.claim_text: Adding semantic edges to co-occurrence networks is controlled by a cosine similarity threshold; the optimal threshold was dataset-dependent (0.7 for Cookie Theft, 0.4 for Cinderella and ABCD).
identified_claims.section_anchor: 3 Modeling and Characterizing Texts as Complex Networks; 5 Experiments and Results
evidence: Section 3: method described to add edge when cosine similarity > threshold.
Section 5: reports thresholds selected: 0.7 for Cookie Theft and 0.4 for Cinderella and ABCD.
uncertainty_flags: No accuracy-vs-threshold curves or sensitivity analyses presented.
Unclear whether thresholds were selected within a nested CV loop or optimized on full data (risk of optimistic bias if not nested).

identified_claims.claim_text: Preprocessing removes stopwords, punctuation, filled pauses, short false starts and repetitions; lemmatization was intentionally omitted to avoid POS tagging errors in disfluent transcripts.
identified_claims.section_anchor: 3 Modeling and Characterizing Texts as Complex Networks; 4.1.1, 4.1.2 data descriptions
evidence: Section 3: statement that stopwords and punctuation are removed and lemmatization omitted (with rationale citing Machicao et al. 2016).
Section 4.1.1/4.1.2: authors state they automatically removed filled pauses and short false starts following TalkBank guidelines.
uncertainty_flags: Exact stopword list and specifics of filled-pause/false-start removal are not provided; reproducibility concerns.
If filled pauses or punctuation patterns are diagnostic, their removal could reduce or alter classification signal—no ablation quantifies this.

identified_claims.claim_text: Ten network topological measurements are computed and summarized via mean, standard deviation, and skewness to form features for classification.
identified_claims.section_anchor: 4.2.1 Topological Characterization of Networks
evidence: Section 4.2.1 lists 10 metrics (PageRank, Betweenness, Eccentricity, Eigenvector centrality, Average Degree of Neighbors, Average Shortest Path Length, Degree, Assortativity Degree, Diameter, Clustering Coefficient) and states aggregation by µ, σ and γ for local measures.
uncertainty_flags: Feature vector dimensionality not explicitly stated; potential multicollinearity not discussed.
Alternative aggregation statistics (medians, percentiles) not explored; discriminatory power of chosen aggregations is assumed rather than demonstrated.

identified_claims.claim_text: Four classifiers were trained and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation; majority vote ensembles and multi-view learning were used for combinations.
identified_claims.section_anchor: 4.3 Classification Algorithms; 5 Experiments and Results
evidence: Section 4.3: lists classifiers (GaussianNB, KNN, SVM linear and RBF, Random Forest) and ensemble/multi-view descriptions.
Section 5: notes experiments used scikit-learn and 5-fold CV; tables report per-classifier accuracies.
uncertainty_flags: Hyperparameter tuning (SVM C/gamma, RF number of trees, KNN k) is not detailed; unclear whether tuning was nested within CV.
No report of SD or per-fold accuracies; single aggregated accuracy values limit ability to assess variability and significance.

strengths.title: Well-motivated representation for noisy short texts
strengths.description: The paper identifies the problem of near-linear co-occurrence networks for short/disfluent transcripts and proposes a conceptually simple enrichment with semantic edges to densify graphs and recover semantic signal.
evidence: Section 3 motivates enrichment citing Amancio (2015c) and illustrates enriched vs. raw co-occurrence graphs (Figure 2).
Use of Perozzi et al. (2014) style induced networks adapted to short clinical narratives.

strengths.title: Multilingual, multi-dataset empirical evaluation
strengths.description: Experiments cover English (DementiaBank Cookie Theft) and Portuguese datasets (Cinderella and ABCD), including both manually processed and automatically segmented transcripts, increasing external relevance.
evidence: Section 4.1 describes the three datasets and provides both automatic and manually processed variants for Cinderella.
Tables 4–7 present results across all datasets and variants.

strengths.title: Practical, lightweight pipeline
strengths.description: The pipeline avoids parser-dependent preprocessing (no lemmatization/POS) and uses language-agnostic network features combined with subword embeddings for OOV robustness, suiting automated/low-resource settings.
evidence: Section 3 explains omission of lemmatization due to disfluencies and cites TalkBank guidelines for filled-pause removal.
Section 4.2.1 choice of Bojanowski embeddings explicitly justified for OOV handling.

concerns.title: No uncertainty quantification for reported accuracies
concerns.description: Accuracy numbers are presented as single point estimates (tables) without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical tests; this prevents assessing whether reported differences (CNE vs LM/BoW or ensemble gains) are significant or within sampling noise.
evidence: Tables 4–7 show single accuracy values per classifier/feature set without SD/CI.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers flagged the absence of variance/CI repeatedly.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report per-fold accuracies and standard deviations (or use repeated CV/bootstrapping), and perform statistical comparisons (e.g., paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank, McNemar test on predictions or permutation tests) between CNE and baselines; include confidence intervals for ensemble gains.

concerns.title: Potential data leakage in threshold and hyperparameter selection
concerns.description: Threshold for adding semantic edges and any classifier hyperparameter tuning are described but it's unclear whether these were optimized in a nested fashion within cross-validation; tuning on all data risks overestimating performance.
evidence: Section 5 reports optimized thresholds per dataset but does not state nested CV for threshold/hyperparameter selection.
Prior-stage digest repeatedly noted risk of leakage.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify and, if necessary, re-run experiments using nested CV where threshold and classifier hyperparameters are selected only on training folds; report results obtained with proper nesting and compare to original numbers.

concerns.title: Insufficient ablation isolating embedding and preprocessing effects
concerns.description: The mechanism by which CNE yields gains is not isolated: no ablation compares subword embeddings vs other embeddings (standard skip-gram, pretrained fastText) or quantifies OOV rates; preprocessing choices (filled-pause removal, stopword list, no lemmatization) may differentially affect feature spaces and remain untested.
evidence: Section 4.2.1 mentions Bojanowski embeddings and default training params but no comparison to alternatives.
Shared analysis notes absence of OOV statistics and ablation beyond CN vs CNE.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add ablation experiments: (a) compare Bojanowski embeddings to skip-gram, pretrained fastText, and random embeddings; (b) report OOV rates and show how subword embeddings change similarity distributions for frequent OOVs; (c) test keeping vs removing filled pauses and including lemmatization to assess their impact on CNE and LM.

concerns.title: Limited description of preprocessing and reproducibility details
concerns.description: Key reproducibility choices are underspecified: exact stopword list, tokenization rules, scripts for filled-pause/false-start removal, whether graphs are weighted/unweighted, and full feature vector dimensionality/normalization are not provided.
evidence: Sections mention stopword and punctuation removal and TalkBank guidelines but do not provide lists or code.
Topological feature aggregation described but not full dimensionality per document.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide preprocessing scripts or append explicit lists (stopwords, filled-pause tokens), state whether networks are weighted and how semantic edges are added (binary or weighted by cosine), give full feature vector dimensionality, and include code or pseudo-code for feature extraction.

concerns.title: Aggregations and feature engineering limited
concerns.description: Only mean, standard deviation and skewness are used to summarize node-level measures; other descriptive statistics (median, percentiles) or node-level patterns may capture discriminative signal lost by these three moments.
evidence: Section 4.2.1 states µ(X), σ(X), and γ(X) computed for local measures, alternative aggregations not explored.
Shared analysis suggested potential missed distributional signals.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include additional aggregations (median, interquartile range, selected percentiles), and consider node-level embedding of key nodes (e.g., top-k PageRank nodes) or use graph-level representation learning (graph2vec, WL kernels) as ablations.

concerns.title: Ensemble/multi-view description and validation underspecified
concerns.description: The majority-vote ensembles and multi-view combinations are reported but methodological details (whether combination uses out-of-fold predictions, how ties are handled, whether ensembles use calibrated probabilities) are absent, limiting interpretation of ensemble gains.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes majority vote and multi-view at a high level; Section 5 reports ensemble accuracies without procedural details.
Shared analysis flagged lack of fold-level detail for ensembles.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Describe ensemble/multi-view combination procedure precisely: whether predictions combined per-fold using out-of-sample predictions, tie-breaking rules, and whether probabilistic calibration was applied; compare majority vote to stacking or weighted voting (learned weights) as ablations.

comparable_works.relevance: Methodological precedent for inducing networks from word embeddings; authors adapt this idea to enrich co-occurrence networks.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: both induce graph structure from continuous embeddings; Difference: this paper combines embedding-based edges with co-occurrence adjacency specifically for short clinical transcripts and computes aggregated topological measures for classification.
comparable_works.source_trace: References and Section 3 referencing Perozzi et al. (2014)

comparable_works.relevance: Embedding method used (subword-aware) to mitigate OOV in short/disfluent transcripts.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Directly used by authors; prior work demonstrates subword benefits vs standard skip-gram in syntactic tasks but mixed on semantics.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior work showing short texts lead to near-linear networks with limited topological signal, motivating enrichment.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides the empirical/analytical motivation for enrichment; this paper operationalizes the fix via embedding edges.

comparable_works.citation_label: Fraser et al., 2015; Roark et al., 2011; Vincze et al., 2016
comparable_works.relevance: Representative prior clinical studies using linguistic and acoustic features for dementia/MCI detection; used as performance context (60–85%).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: These works rely on linguistic/parser-dependent or acoustic features; the present paper proposes an alternative robust to disfluencies.

uncertainty_flags: Absence of per-fold variance/CI for accuracies — hard to know if differences are statistically meaningful.
Unclear whether threshold optimization and classifier hyperparameter tuning were nested within CV — potential data leakage.
Small sample sizes (especially Cinderella) increase variance and risk that reported improvements are dataset-specific.
No explicit OOV statistics or embedding-comparison ablation — mechanism for CNE gains is partially speculative.
Preprocessing (filled pause removal, no lemmatization) could remove diagnostic cues; impacts not quantified.
alternative_interpretations: Observed CNE gains may partly reflect overfitting due to threshold tuning or hyperparameter selection performed on the whole dataset rather than nested CV.
Preprocessing (removing filled pauses or stopwords) might differentially reduce LM performance more than CNE, making CNE seem better primarily because LM lost informative cues during cleaning.
Majority-vote ensemble gains might follow from variance reduction across classifiers rather than complementarity of feature spaces; stacking/weighted voting could show different results.

CNE improvements could stem mainly from densification (increasing graph connectivity) that incidentally correlates with target labels (e.g., MCI narratives shorter/more repetitive), rather than capturing meaningful semantic relations.
transparency_notes: The manuscript provides embedding training parameters (100 dim, window 5, epochs 5) but omits training corpus sizes and vocabulary/OOV counts.
Threshold values selected per dataset are reported but the selection procedure (grid search range, validation protocol) is not documented.
Preprocessing policy is described at a high level (stopword removal, filled pauses removed) but exact token lists and scripts are not included.
Classifier hyperparameter tuning protocols (search ranges, nested CV) and whether features were normalized/scaled are not specified.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The approach—enriching co-occurrence networks for short clinical transcripts with subword-aware embeddings and extracting aggregated topological features—is not widely represented in the retrieved literature; sparse precedent suggests novelty but does not validate empirical claims without stronger statistical controls and ablation.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If threshold and classifier hyperparameters are selected strictly within training folds (nested CV) and results remain similar with reported effect sizes and low variance, the method likely generalizes.
If ablations show Bojanowski embeddings materially reduce OOV and that alternative embeddings (pretrained fastText or skip-gram) perform worse, this would support the subword OOV mechanism.
If keeping filled pauses or adding lemmatization does not materially change CNE performance but improves LM, the robustness claim for CNE is strengthened.
If repeated CV or bootstrapping yields stable ensemble gains across datasets (Cinderella, ABCD, Cookie Theft), the reported multi-view benefits are reliable rather than dataset artifacts.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The core idea adapts established methods (word-embedding induced graphs and co-occurrence networks) to a new problem (MCI detection from short/disfluent transcripts) and combines them with standard aggregated graph measures. The adaptation to subword-aware embeddings for OOV-rich clinical transcripts is sensible and practically motivated.
evidence: Cites Perozzi et al. (2014) for embedding-induced networks and Bojanowski et al. (2016) for subword embeddings; applies these in a new pipeline for clinical short texts.
uncertainty_flags: Mechanistic contributions (why Bojanowski specifically helps here) are not empirically isolated; novelty is at methodological adaptation rather than a disruptive paradigm shift.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Applying this enrichment pipeline across English and Portuguese datasets and including both manual and automatic transcript variants addresses an important practical need (language independence and robustness to ASR-like transcripts).
evidence: Experiments on DementiaBank (English) and two Portuguese datasets (Cinderella and ABCD) with automatic segmentation and manual correction variants.
uncertainty_flags: Generality across more datasets and larger cohorts remains to be demonstrated; current sample sizes are modest.

confidence_interval.rationale: Overall confidence in the main empirical claims is moderate but bounded by methodological gaps. The lower bound reflects risks from potential hyperparameter leakage, lack of variance reporting, and small datasets; the upper bound reflects consistent point-estimate results across multiple datasets and a coherent methodological rationale. Re-running experiments with nested tuning, reporting per-fold variance, and providing ablations could move the interval substantially upward.

consensus_findings: The paper proposes enriching word-adjacency (co-occurrence) networks with subword-aware word embeddings (Bojanowski et al.) by adding semantic edges above a cosine-similarity threshold (CNE) and extracting aggregated topological features (mean, std, skew) to classify MCI vs. controls.

CNE typically attains point-estimate accuracies that are competitive with or higher than co-occurrence-only networks (CN), Coh-Metrix-derived linguistic metrics (LM), and simple Bag-of-Words (BoW) baselines in the reported experiments across the three datasets.

The authors evaluated the approach on multiple datasets (English: Cookie Theft / DementiaBank; Portuguese: Cinderella and ABCD), including manual and automatically segmented transcript variants, which strengthens the empirical scope compared to a single-corpus study.

Preprocessing choices were made to favor a lightweight, parser-free pipeline (removing stopwords/punctuation and many filled-pause tokens; no lemmatization), motivated by disfluency-induced parser fragility.

Ensemble and multi-view combinations (majority-vote) of feature spaces often increase the reported point-estimate accuracy compared to single-feature classifiers in some datasets (notably Cinderella and ABCD).
disagreements: Degree of empirical robustness: reviewers agree CNE shows promising point-wise gains but disagree on how credible the quantitative superiority is without variance estimates and nested tuning. Some treat the table trends as meaningful signals (novel/adaptive method), others emphasize high risk of over-optimism due to methodological reporting gaps.

Novelty weight: some reviewers frame the contribution as a useful, moderately novel methodological adaptation (composition of known elements applied to a new domain); at least one reviewer emphasizes this as a potentially disruptive, practically valuable conceptual move. The disagreement is about degree of novelty (incremental vs. notable innovation), not about the existence of any novelty.

Preprocessing impact: reviewers differ on how concerning the removal of filled pauses and stopwords is. Some consider it a reasonable pragmatic choice for an automated pipeline; others highlight that these tokens may themselves be diagnostic and that their removal could bias comparisons (harm LM more than CNE).

Sufficiency of baselines: some reviewers find Coh-Metrix + BoW acceptable as baselines for this work; others argue stronger modern baselines (pretrained fastText, contextual embeddings, BERT-derived representations) should be included to contextualize CNE performance.
uncertainty_hotspots: No variance / uncertainty reporting: reported accuracies are single aggregated numbers (5-fold mean) without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests — critical for assessing robustness, especially given small datasets (e.g., Cinderella).

Hyperparameter and threshold tuning protocol: it is unclear whether the cosine-threshold for adding semantic edges and classifier hyperparameters were selected inside a nested cross-validation (risk of leakage and optimistic estimates).

Mechanism of improvement: absence of ablations comparing embedding types (Bojanowski subword vs. skip-gram vs. pretrained fastText vs. random embeddings) and no reported OOV statistics leave mechanistic claims (subword OOV mitigation drives gains) only partially supported.

Preprocessing choices: removal of filled pauses, stopwords, and omission of lemmatization were not ablated; these choices may have removed diagnostically relevant signals and differentially affected LM/BoW, confounding comparisons.
Threshold sensitivity and stability: only a single optimized threshold per dataset is reported (0.7 vs 0.4), with no sensitivity plots or stability analysis across folds and seeds.

Ensemble/multi-view methodology: description of majority-vote aggregation lacks fold-level procedural detail (out-of-fold combination vs. global), weighting/tie rules, and comparisons to stacking/weighted voting; reported ensemble gains therefore have uncertain provenance.
model_diversity_effects: Multiple reviewer perspectives (structure/logical, reproducibility/methodology, incremental and disruptive novelty lenses, claim verification) produced complementary emphases: structural reviewers highlighted logical coherence and gaps in mechanistic isolation; methodology-focused reviewers emphasized reproducibility (nested CV, variance reporting); novelty assessors stressed the practical value of the integration and domain adaptation; claim verifiers focused on evidence vs. stated claims.

This diversity surfaces non-overlapping but important concerns: (a) logical justification that enrichment should help short texts, (b) reproducibility controls to ensure effects are not artifacts, and (c) novelty-context needs (which baselines to include). Combining these points leads to pragmatic next steps (nested CV, ablations, CI/p-values, stronger baselines).

Role-specific effects matter: reviewers focused on methodology (reproducibility) are more sensitive to protocol leakage and variance reporting; novelty assessors are more tolerant of incremental reuse of known components but demand empirical rigor to support broader claims; the structure analyst ties these into a coherent argument graph showing where assumptions feed conclusions.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Center questions for editorial decision-making (do not use as accept/reject): (1) Are the reported empirical gains sufficiently substantiated with robust experimental protocol and uncertainty quantification? If not, request revisions focused on statistical and reproducibility rigor. (2) Ask authors to clarify whether threshold and classifier hyperparameter selection were nested inside cross-validation; if not, request nested CV re-runs or a held-out test set. (3) Require reporting of per-fold results (means and SDs), confidence intervals, and at least one paired statistical comparison (e.g., permutation test or Wilcoxon signed-rank) between the main proposed method (CNE) and the primary baselines (LM, CN, BoW). (4) Request transparency artifacts: preprocessing scripts (stopword list, filled-pause removal rules), embedding training code and seeds, network construction code, and CV split seeds to enable reproducibility. (5) Encourage targeted ablations prior to final evaluation: embedding-type comparison and OOV statistics, effect of keeping vs removing filled pauses, and threshold sensitivity plots. These targeted checks will enable the editor to assess whether CNE's empirical claims generalize beyond dataset-specific artifacts.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and address reviewer concerns, provide the following revisions and additions: (1) Experimental protocol transparency: explicitly state whether threshold search and classifier hyperparameter tuning were done inside a nested CV. If not, re-run experiments with nested CV (inner loop for tuning, outer loop for evaluation) or report results on a held-out test set. (2) Uncertainty quantification: report per-fold accuracies for all experiments, plus mean ± standard deviation and 95% confidence intervals (consider repeated CV, e.g., 10x5-fold or bootstrap) and include paired statistical tests comparing CNE against CN, LM and BoW. (3) Ablation studies: (a) compare Bojanowski subword embeddings to at least one alternative (standard skip-gram and/or pretrained fastText/word2vec) and a random-permuted-embedding baseline; (b) report OOV rates and show how OOV handling changes semantic-edge counts; (c) perform CN vs CNE ablation across embedding choices. (4) Preprocessing sensitivity: run and report experiments keeping vs removing filled pauses and with/without lemmatization to show how preprocessing choices affect each feature family. (5) Threshold analysis: provide accuracy vs cosine-threshold curves and quantify the stability range; report average number of semantic edges added per transcript at chosen thresholds. (6) Ensemble/multi-view detail: state exactly how majority votes are formed (whether using out-of-fold predictions), how ties are handled, and compare to at least one alternative fusion strategy (stacking or weighted voting). (7) Reproducibility package: publish preprocessing scripts and lists (stopwords, filled-pause tokens), embedding training code and resulting vectors, network construction scripts, feature extraction code, classifier hyperparameters and seeds, and CV splits (or code to reproduce them). (8) Optionally, include a stronger baseline using sentence / contextual embeddings (e.g., averaged BERT or pretrained sentence embeddings) to situate CNE relative to modern embedding-based baselines. Addressing these points will reduce ambiguity about mechanism and increase confidence in generalization.
transparency_report: Existing transparency: authors report embedding training parameters (model choice Bojanowski et al., 100 dimensions, window=5, epochs=5) and state optimized cosine-threshold values per dataset (0.7 for Cookie Theft; 0.4 for Cinderella and ABCD). They list the ten topological measures computed and the four classifiers used.

Missing or insufficient details requested by reviewers: (a) whether threshold and classifier hyperparameter tuning were nested within cross-validation; (b) per-fold accuracies, standard deviations, and confidence intervals; (c) exact preprocessing artifacts (stopword list, filled-pause/false-start removal rules, tokenization); (d) embedding training data size, vocab/OOV counts, random seeds, and trained vector files; (e) network construction code (whether semantic edges are binary or weighted, whether graphs are directed/undirected/weighted); (f) classifier hyperparameter ranges and final settings; (g) ensemble/multi-view combination procedure (out-of-fold vs global, tie-breaking, weighting).

Reproducibility recommendations: provide a code and data release (or appendix) including preprocessing scripts, embedding training and saved models, network construction and feature extraction scripts, CV split seeds, per-fold predictions, and configuration files for classifiers so experiments can be exactly reproduced.
epistemic_limits: The current evidence base in the manuscript supports the plausibility of CNE as a promising representation for noisy, short clinical transcripts, but the lack of uncertainty quantification, unclear tuning procedures (possible leakage), limited ablations (no embedding-type comparison or OOV quantification), and underspecified preprocessing constrain strong inferential claims about superiority or generalizability. Reported point-estimate accuracy differences could be (a) genuine and generalizable, (b) artifacts of threshold/hyperparameter selection on the full data, (c) consequences of preprocessing choices that differentially affect baselines, or (d) variance-driven fluctuations on small datasets. Until the authors supply nested evaluation, variance estimates, and targeted ablations, confidence in the mechanistic interpretation (that subword embeddings specifically confer OOV-driven advantages leading to better topology features) remains provisional.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes enriching word-adjacency (co-occurrence) networks derived from speech transcripts with subword-aware word embeddings (Bojanowski et al., 2016) by adding semantic edges above a cosine-similarity threshold (CNE), extracting aggregated topological features (mean, SD, skewness of 10 node measures), and using standard classifiers (SVM, RF, KNN, GaussianNB) to distinguish MCI from controls. Experiments on three datasets (English DementiaBank Cookie Theft; Portuguese Cinderella and ABCD, with manual and automatic transcript variants) report that CNE often yields higher point-estimate accuracies than co-occurrence-only networks (CN), Coh-Metrix-derived linguistic metrics, and Bag-of-Words; ensemble / multi-view majority-vote combinations sometimes further improve accuracy.
strengths: Clear, pragmatic motivation: addresses parser fragility on short, disfluent clinical transcripts and proposes a lightweight, language-agnostic representation.

Methodological adaptation: combines co-occurrence networks with embedding-derived semantic edges (subword-aware embeddings) to densify short-text graphs—a conceptually coherent fix to near-linear networks.
Multilingual empirical scope: evaluation across English and Portuguese datasets (including manual and automatic transcript variants) increases application relevance beyond single-corpus studies.
Reasonable baseline set: compares CNE against co-occurrence only, Coh-Metrix / Coh-Metrix-Dementia linguistic metrics and BoW, and reports multiple classifiers and ensemble combinations.
limitations: No uncertainty quantification: reported classification results are single aggregated accuracy figures (5-fold means) without per-fold values, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or formal statistical tests—this impedes assessment of robustness on small samples (e.g., Cinderella).

Unclear tuning protocol with potential data leakage: manuscript reports 'optimized' cosine-thresholds per dataset (0.7 / 0.4) but does not state whether threshold and classifier hyperparameter selection were nested within cross-validation; if not, performance estimates may be optimistic.

Insufficient ablation for mechanism: the claimed role of subword-aware embeddings (OOV mitigation) is not isolated—no comparison to alternative embeddings (skip-gram, pretrained fastText, random vectors) and no reporting of OOV rates or the number of semantic edges added by enrichment.

Preprocessing choices under-specified and potentially confounding: automatic removal of stopwords, filled pauses and omission of lemmatization are described but exact lists/rules are not provided and no experiments test whether keeping those markers alters relative performance of CNE vs linguistic baselines.
open_questions: Were cosine-threshold selection and classifier hyperparameter tuning performed inside an inner (nested) cross-validation loop, or were they optimized on the entire dataset prior to reporting 5-fold CV results? Please describe the exact tuning protocol.

Please provide per-fold accuracies (or repeated CV results) and corresponding standard deviations / 95% confidence intervals for all reported rows (CN, CNE, LM, BoW, ensembles) and include at least one paired statistical test comparing CNE to the main baselines.

Can authors provide ablation results comparing Bojanowski subword embeddings to (a) standard skip-gram trained on the same corpus, (b) pretrained fastText/word2vec, and (c) random/permuted embeddings, along with OOV counts and the average number of semantic edges added per transcript at chosen thresholds?

How do preprocessing choices affect results? Please report experiments (or at least a targeted analysis) keeping vs removing filled pauses and with/without lemmatization to show whether such choices differentially impact LM, BoW and CNE.

Describe ensemble/multi-view combination in fold-level detail: were majority votes formed using out-of-fold predictions per training split, how were ties handled, and were any alternative fusion strategies (stacking, weighted voting) tried?
consensus_snapshot: CNE (co-occurrence networks enriched with embeddings) is a plausible, well-motivated representation that often attains higher point-estimate accuracies than CN, Coh-Metrix-derived linguistic metrics and basic BoW in the reported tables.

The methodological idea—densifying short co-occurrence graphs using embedding-derived semantic edges, with subword embeddings to mitigate OOV—addresses a genuine short-text limitation and is an interesting adaptation for noisy clinical transcripts.

Reproducibility and statistical robustness are the main missing elements: reviewers consistently ask for nested tuning, variance estimates, ablation with alternative embeddings and transparent preprocessing code.
disagreement_snapshot: Degree of novelty: some reviewers treat the contribution as a useful incremental methodological adaptation (combining known components) while others see the composition and application to clinical short-texts as a practically notable innovation. The substantive disagreement concerns how novel the integration is (incremental vs practically innovative), not whether the approach is logically coherent.

Interpretation of point-estimate gains: reviewers agree CNE shows pointwise advantages, but they disagree on credibility—some view the trends as meaningful signals warranting further validation, others caution that without nested CV and variance reporting the gains might be artifacts of tuning or preprocessing choices.
uncertainty_snapshot: Primary epistemic uncertainty arises from lack of variance reporting and unclear nesting of hyperparameter and threshold tuning (possible optimistic bias).

Mechanistic uncertainty: absence of embedding-type ablations and OOV statistics leaves open whether subword modeling specifically drives improvements versus generic densification or increased model capacity.

Operational uncertainty: insufficient detail on preprocessing (stopword/filler lists, tokenization), network weighting (binary vs weighted edges), feature dimensionality, and ensemble formation rules hinders reproducibility and interpretation.
source_trace: Perozzi et al., 2014 — inducing language networks from continuous-space word representations: motivates building graphs from embeddings (manuscript Section 3 and shared analysis).
Bojanowski et al., 2016 (fastText / subword embeddings): cited as the embedding method used to mitigate OOV and handle morphological variants (manuscript Section 4.2.1 and shared analysis).

Amancio (2015c) and related work on short-text network limitations: provides the observation that short texts generate near-linear networks, motivating enrichment (manuscript Section 3 and shared analysis).
Graesser et al., 2004 (Coh-Metrix) and Coh-Metrix-Dementia: sources of linguistic baseline features used and discussed in comparisons (manuscript Section 4.2.2 and shared analysis).
transparency_notes: Authors report embedding training parameters (model choice: Bojanowski subword, 100 dimensions, window=5, epochs=5) and final cosine thresholds per dataset (0.7 for Cookie Theft; 0.4 for Cinderella and ABCD). Missing critical reproducibility details include: (a) whether threshold and classifier hyperparameter tuning were nested within cross-validation and the search grids used; (b) per-fold accuracies and random seeds; (c) exact preprocessing scripts (stopword list, filled-pause tokens, tokenization rules); (d) embedding training corpus sizes, vocabulary/OOV counts and trained vector files; (e) network construction code (directed/undirected, binary vs weighted semantic edges) and final feature vector dimensionality; (f) classifier hyperparameters and normalization steps; (g) ensemble/multi-view fold-level procedure (out-of-fold predictions, tie-breaking rules). Providing code and these artifacts (or a reproducibility appendix) is strongly recommended.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request a revision that focuses on reproducibility and robustness checks before relying on the reported quantitative claims. Specifically ask the authors to (1) clarify and, if needed, re-run experiments with nested cross-validation for threshold and classifier hyperparameter selection (inner loop tuning, outer loop evaluation) or provide held-out test set results; (2) provide per-fold accuracies, standard deviations and 95% confidence intervals, and at least one paired statistical test comparing CNE against principal baselines; (3) include ablation experiments comparing embedding types (Bojanowski subword vs standard skip-gram vs pretrained fastText vs random) and report OOV statistics and semantic-edge counts; (4) supply preprocessing scripts/lists and explain which Coh-Metrix metrics were excluded for parser fragility; (5) detail ensemble/multi-view voting implementations and consider at least one alternative fusion strategy (stacking or learned weights). These targeted revisions address the main methodological uncertainties and will materially strengthen the manuscript's evidentiary basis.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and reproducibility, please provide the following in a revision or appendix: (1) Exact experimental protocol: state whether threshold and hyperparameter tuning were nested within cross-validation; if not, re-run with nested CV or a held-out test split and report revisions. (2) Uncertainty reporting: per-fold accuracies, mean ± SD, 95% CIs, and paired statistical comparisons (e.g., permutation test or Wilcoxon) comparing CNE vs CN, LM and BoW. (3) Embedding ablations: include at least skip-gram and pretrained fastText (or similar) and a random-permutation baseline; report OOV rates and how many semantic edges were added per transcript at each threshold. (4) Preprocessing transparency and sensitivity: publish stopword/filler lists and preprocessing code and run experiments keeping vs removing filled pauses and with/without lemmatization to show sensitivity. (5) Threshold sensitivity: provide accuracy vs threshold curves and show stability ranges. (6) Ensemble details: describe fold-level voting procedure (out-of-fold prediction aggregation), tie rules, and compare to stacking or weighted voting. (7) Release reproducibility artifacts: preprocessing scripts, embedding training code and vectors, graph construction and feature extraction code, classifier configurations and CV split seeds. Optionally, add a modern embedding baseline (sentence/contextual embeddings) to contextualize relative gains. These steps will clarify mechanism, reduce leakage risk, and increase confidence in generalization.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper introduces CNE: co-occurrence networks enriched with subword-aware embeddings to densify short, disfluent speech-transcript graphs and extract aggregated topological features for MCI detection. Experiments across English and Portuguese datasets report that CNE often yields higher point-estimate accuracies than co-occurrence-only networks, Coh-Metrix-derived linguistic metrics, and simple BoW; ensemble/multi-view majority-vote combinations sometimes further improve accuracy.

Strengths:
- Addresses a real practical problem (parser fragility on disfluent clinical transcripts) with a lightweight, language-agnostic approach.
- Conceptually coherent adaptation: embedding-derived semantic edges mitigate near-linear topology in short texts.
- Multilingual evaluation and comparative baselines increase applied relevance.

Limitations:
- Lack of uncertainty quantification: no per-fold accuracies, SDs or confidence intervals are reported; statistical significance is not tested. This is critical given small datasets and modest absolute gains.
- Possible methodological leakage: it is unclear whether cosine-thresholds and classifier hyperparameters were tuned inside training folds (nested CV). Non-nested tuning could inflate reported accuracies.
- Mechanistic ambiguity: no ablations comparing Bojanowski subword embeddings to alternatives (standard skip-gram, pretrained fastText, random vectors) and no OOV statistics—so the claimed subword OOV advantage is not empirically isolated.
- Preprocessing confound: automatic removal of filled pauses/stopwords and omission of lemmatization are underspecified and may remove diagnostic signals; their differential effect on LM vs CNE is untested.

Open Questions:
1) Were thresholds and classifier hyperparameters optimized within a nested CV inner loop or on the full dataset? Please detail the hyperparameter search grids and CV nesting.
2) Please provide per-fold results (or repeated CV results) with mean ± SD and 95% CIs for all reported methods and run at least one paired statistical test comparing CNE to CN and LM.
3) Can you present ablations comparing Bojanowski subword embeddings to standard skip-gram, pretrained fastText/word2vec, and a random embeddings baseline, together with OOV counts and average number of semantic edges added per transcript? 
4) How sensitive are results to preprocessing choices (keeping vs removing filled pauses; applying lemmatization)? Please report those comparisons.
5) Precisely how were ensembles/multi-view votes formed at fold-level (out-of-fold predictions vs global training), and were alternative fusion methods (stacking/weighted voting) tried?

Transparency:
Authors report embedding training params (Bojanowski, 100-D, window=5, epochs=5) and final thresholds per dataset; however missing items include per-fold accuracies and variance, explicit CV nesting statement, preprocessing scripts (stopword/filler lists), embedding vocab/OOV stats and trained vectors, graph construction code (binary/weighted, directedness), feature dimensionality and normalization, classifier hyperparameter configs, and ensemble voting procedure. Providing these artifacts (code + configs + seeds) is strongly recommended.

Epistemic/ Retrieval limits:
This synthesis is grounded in the manuscript excerpts, the shared analysis and specialist reviews. I relied on cited methods (Perozzi et al., Bojanowski et al., Amancio) as contextual traces; I did not re-run experiments nor access the authors' code or datasets. Consequently, claims about possible leakage, OOV statistics, and sensitivity are inferential based on reporting gaps rather than confirmed protocol errors.

Overall assessment guidance (no decision):
CNE is a promising, well-motivated methodological adaptation with supportive point-estimate empirical results across multiple datasets. However, the manuscript requires targeted methodological clarifications and reproducibility/robustness analyses (nested CV for tuning, variance reporting, embedding ablations, preprocessing sensitivity, ensemble protocol details, and code release) to substantiate claims about generality and mechanism. Addressing these points will materially increase confidence in the findings and their practical applicability.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects moderate support for the conceptual idea (embedding-enriched networks for short/disfluent clinical transcripts) and consistent point-estimate results across datasets, tempered by substantial methodological/reporting gaps (missing variance estimates, unclear nested tuning, absent ablations, underspecified preprocessing) that materially affect confidence in quantitative claims and generalizability.

They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Section: 🆕 4. Check for common problems in NLP papers
Codes: M1, G2
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor
Content: As a counter to common problems with reviews, there are also common problems with NLP papers. We do ask you to watch out for these and point them out when you see them. Above all else, published research should at least be technically sound and appropriately scoped. There are several data sets to assess how well a DSM captures human intuitions about semantic relatedness, such as the Rubenstein and Goodenough set (Rubenstein & Goode- nough, 1965) and WordSim353 (Finkelstein, Gabrilovich, Matias, Rivlin, Solan, Wolfman, & Ruppin, 2002). Usually they are constructed by asking subjects to rate a set of word pairs according to a similarity scale. Then, the average rating for each pair is taken as an estimate of the perceived relatedness between the words (e.g.,dollar-buck: 9.22,cord-smile: 0.31). To measure how well a distributional model approximates human semantic intuitions, usually a correlation measure between the similarity scores generated by the model and the human ratings is computed. The highest correlation we are aware of on the WordSim353 set we will also employ below is of 0.80 and it was obtained by a model called Temporal Semantic Analysis, which captures patterns of word usage over time and where concepts are represented as time series over a corpus of temporally-ordered documents (Radinsky, Agichtein, Gabrilovich, & Markovitch, 2011). top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
